Augusta GA Fishing Spots: The Local’s Guide to the Savannah River & Beyond

If you’re searching for the best Augusta GA fishing spots, you’ve come to the right place. Augusta sits on the banks of the Savannah River and within easy reach of Clarks Hill Lake (J. Strom Thurmond Lake), offering anglers a mix of moving water and big-reservoir action. Whether you’re chasing striped bass in the tailrace, largemouth in the back of a creek, or bream on a quiet bank, this guide covers the spots, the seasons, and the local know-how to make your trip count.

1. Savannah River (Downtown Augusta & the Riverwalk)

The Savannah River is the heart of Augusta fishing. The stretch through downtown—from the New Savannah Bluff Lock and Dam down past the Riverwalk—holds a surprising variety of fish. You’ll find striped bass, hybrid bass, largemouth, catfish, and even the occasional trout in cooler months.

Where to fish

  • Riverwalk & 5th Street Bridge area: Bank access is easy, and the current seams near the bridge pilings attract striped bass. Fish early morning or late evening for best results.
  • New Savannah Bluff Lock and Dam: The tailrace below the dam is a proven spot for striped bass and hybrid. Access is from the Georgia side off Lock and Dam Road; watch for generation schedules.
  • Augusta Canal: The canal’s slower water holds largemouth and panfish, and it’s a great option when the river is high or muddy.

Local tip

For a unique stay with direct river access, consider KJ Augusta Rentals’ Entire River House—it sits on three private acres right on the Savannah River, with a private dock and boat slip. You can be on the water at first light without driving anywhere.

2. Clarks Hill Lake (J. Strom Thurmond Lake)

About 30 minutes north of Augusta, Clarks Hill Lake is the region’s premier big-water fishery. At over 70,000 acres, it’s known for largemouth bass, striped bass, crappie, and catfish. Spring and fall are prime; summer fishing shifts to deep structure and night trips.

Best access points

  • Wildwood Park: Excellent ramps, picnic areas, and bank fishing. Good for families and first-timers.
  • Cherokee Boat Ramp: Quiet access on the Georgia side; nearby coves hold crappie in spring.
  • Lake Springs Recreation Area: Off Highway 221; a good base for bass and catfish.

What’s biting

Spring: largemouth shallow in coves; crappie around brush. Summer: striped bass deep near the dam; catfish at night. Fall: bass schooling on points. Winter: crappie and bass deep on jigs.

3. Butler Creek & Other Tributaries

Butler Creek, on the Georgia side of Clarks Hill, is a local favorite for crappie and bass, especially in spring when fish move into the creeks to spawn. The creek’s timber and brush provide cover, and it’s less crowded than the main lake.

Other tributaries worth exploring: Keg Creek, Soap Creek, and Little River. All offer good spring fishing and quieter surroundings.

4. Augusta Canal & Local Ponds

For a quick fix without a boat, the Augusta Canal is hard to beat. It’s stocked with catfish and holds resident largemouth and bream. Access points along the canal towpath (e.g., near the Lake Olmstead Trailhead) are easy and safe. Local ponds like Lake Olmstead and Pendleton King Park pond offer bank fishing for bream and bass—great for kids.

What Fish Are in Season in Georgia? A Quick Primer

Georgia’s warm climate means year-round fishing, but each species has its peak. Here’s what to expect:

  • Largemouth bass: Spring (spawn) and fall. Summer early/late; winter deep.
  • Striped bass: Spring and fall runs in the Savannah River; summer deep in Clarks Hill.
  • Crappie: Spring spawn (March–April) is prime; fall secondary.
  • Catfish: Summer nights and fall.
  • Bream (bluegill, redear): Late spring through summer.

Always check the latest Augusta GA fishing report from local bait shops (e.g., Sportsman’s Corner on Washington Road) or the Georgia DNR for current conditions and regulations.

What Fish Can You Catch in Georgia?

Georgia’s diversity is impressive. In the Augusta area, you can target:

  • Largemouth bass, spotted bass, striped bass, hybrid bass
  • Crappie (black and white), bluegill, redear sunfish
  • Channel catfish, blue catfish, flathead catfish
  • Bowfin, gar, and the occasional chain pickerel in backwaters

For a full list, see the Georgia DNR’s freshwater fishing page.

What Fish Are Biting in Georgia Now? (Seasonal Cheat Sheet)

Fishing reports change weekly, but here’s a general guide by season:

  • Spring (March–May): Bass shallow, crappie spawning, striped bass moving upriver. Topwaters early.
  • Summer (June–August): Early morning and night are best. Bass deep on ledges; catfish biting. Stripers deep near dams.
  • Fall (September–November): Bass schooling on points; stripers active in the river. Crappie start moving to creek mouths.
  • Winter (December–February): Slow but rewarding. Crappie and bass deep on jigs; trout stocked in some areas.

  • Saltwater pool overlooking the river—perfect for cooling off after a hot day.
  • No shared spaces or other guests on-site—the entire property is yours.

Local Resources & Tips

  • Bait & tackle: Sportsman’s Corner (Washington Rd), Academy Sports (Augusta Exchange), and Walmart (various locations).
  • Licenses: Buy online via the Georgia DNR or at local retailers. A Georgia fishing license is required for ages 16+.
  • Boat ramps: Riverwalk (downtown), New Savannah Bluff, Wildwood Park, Cherokee, Lake Springs.
  • Fishing report: Check the Georgia DNR’s weekly report or call local shops.
  • Safety: Watch for currents below the dam; wear a life jacket; file a float plan if going alone.

Whether you’re here for a weekend or a week, Augusta’s fishing scene delivers—and with the right base, your trip becomes unforgettable. Tight lines!
